title: Space Exploration · Episode 2
chapters: Space junk: the litter problem in orbit
Telescopes: our eyes on the universe

units.t: Space Exploration. Episode two.
In this episode: The International Space Station, Space junk: the litter problem in orbit and Telescopes: our eyes on the universe.
Part one. The International Space Station.
Right now, about 400 kilometres above you, people are eating, sleeping and doing experiments while circling Earth every hour and a half.
A home in orbit.
The International Space Station is a large, crewed laboratory about 400 kilometres up, roughly the distance from Perth to Albany, but straight up.
It travels at about 28,000 km/h and circles Earth every 90 minutes, so the crew sees about 16 sunrises and sunsets a day.
The first module launched in November 1998, and people have lived aboard continuously since 2 November 2000.
A whole generation has grown up without a day when humans weren't living in space.
You can see the station yourself, shortly after dusk or before dawn: a bright, steady point of light gliding across the sky, without flashing like a plane.
NASA's free Spot the Station service tells you when.
Built by five partners.
The station was too big to launch in one go.
Over more than a decade, US Space Shuttles and Russian rockets carried up the pieces, and astronauts bolted them together during hundreds of hours of spacewalks.
The finished structure is about 109 metres across, roughly a football field, and weighs around 420,000 kilograms.
Huge solar arrays supply its electricity.
It is often described as the most expensive object ever built, at well over US$100 billion.
Five agencies run it: NASA, Roscosmos, the European Space Agency, Japan's JAXA and the Canadian Space Agency.
Russia provides key modules and propulsion, Japan built the Kibo laboratory, Europe the Columbus lab and Canada the robotic arm, Canadarm2.
Astronauts from more than 20 countries have visited, including Adelaide-born Andy Thomas.
Floating in free fall.
At the station's height, Earth's gravity is still about 90% as strong as on the ground.
Astronauts float because they and the station are in continuous free fall, falling around Earth while moving sideways fast enough to keep missing it.
Scientists call this microgravity.
Water forms wobbling spheres, flames burn as round blue balls and dropped tools drift away.
A typical crew is about seven people.
They sleep in small cabins, zipped into sleeping bags fixed to the wall.
Water is precious: the station recycles moisture from air, washing and even urine, and in 2023 NASA reported about 98% water recovery.
Food comes in pouches, with tortillas popular because they don't make crumbs.
Toilets use airflow instead of gravity.
The Cupola, a seven-windowed dome, is made for photographing Earth.
What space does to bodies.
Weaker bones and muscles are only the start.

Many astronauts on long missions develop swelling at the back of the eye and a slight flattening of the eyeball, a condition NASA calls spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome, and some need stronger glasses afterwards.
Blood volume drops in orbit, so returning crew can feel faint when they first stand up.
Radiation doses are far higher than on the ground.
In NASA's Twins Study, astronaut Scott Kelly spent almost a year on the station while his identical twin, Mark, stayed on Earth.
Researchers found changes in Scott's gene activity, gut bacteria and immune system, most of which returned to normal within months.
Findings like these help plan trips to Mars.
Science, then retirement.
Thousands of experiments have run aboard.
Microgravity lets scientists study things that gravity masks on Earth.
Protein crystals can grow larger and more orderly, helping researchers understand molecules targeted by medicines.
Flames, fluids and new materials behave differently, which improves models used on the ground.
Crews have grown lettuce, chillies and flowers, and ate lettuce grown on the station in 2015.
The Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer, a particle detector on the outside, searches cosmic rays for clues about dark matter.
The ageing ISS is due to retire around 2030 and be steered into a remote part of the Pacific Ocean.
Commercial stations are being developed, and China already operates its own, Tiangong.
The key idea: The ISS orbits about 400 km up at 28,000 km/h and has been continuously crewed since November 2000.
Part two. Space junk: the litter problem in orbit.
Tens of thousands of dead satellites and rocket parts are racing around Earth faster than bullets, and once in 1979 a big piece landed near Esperance.
A fast-moving cloud.
Since Sputnik in 1957, much of what has gone up has stayed there.
Space junk includes dead satellites, used rocket stages, lost tools, flakes of paint and fragments from explosions and collisions.
Agencies track tens of thousands of pieces larger than about a softball, and estimates suggest around a million pieces bigger than a centimetre, plus many millions smaller.
Most sits in low Earth orbit, the busy region used by the International Space Station.
To stay up there, an object travels at about 28,000 kilometres per hour, many times faster than a rifle bullet.
At that speed even a fleck of paint carries surprising energy, and Space Shuttle windows were replaced after being chipped.
The ISS has extra shielding and regularly fires its engines to dodge tracked debris.
Collisions and tests.
On 10 February 2009 a working Iridium satellite hit a dead Russian satellite, Kosmos 2251, about 790 kilometres above Siberia.
It was the first known accidental collision between two intact satellites and created well over a thousand trackable fragments.
In 1978 NASA scientist Donald Kessler warned that if debris became dense enough, collisions would create more fragments, causing more collisions in a cascade.
This is the Kessler syndrome, and in its worst form some orbits could become too risky to use for generations.
Some clouds were made on purpose.
In 2007 China destroyed its own weather satellite with a missile, creating over 3,000 trackable fragments, the largest single event on record.
In 2021 Russia did the same, forcing ISS crew to shelter.
Since 2022 several countries, including Australia, have pledged not to hold such tests.
What goes up.
Thin traces of atmosphere slowly drag on objects in low orbit, so they sink and eventually burn up on re-entry.
Large, sturdy parts can survive.
In July 1979 the American space station Skylab broke apart over the Indian Ocean and scattered debris around Esperance in Western Australia.
Nobody was hurt, and the local shire famously fined NASA $400 for littering.
An American radio host eventually paid it decades later.
In 2022, pieces of a SpaceX capsule's trunk landed on farms in the Snowy Mountains of New South Wales.
Today operators often steer big spacecraft down over a remote part of the South Pacific near Point Nemo, the place furthest from land, nicknamed the spacecraft cemetery.
Crowded skies.
The number of active satellites has soared, mainly because of megaconstellations: huge fleets of small satellites providing internet from low orbit.
SpaceX's Starlink alone has launched many thousands, and others are building their own.
These networks bring fast internet to remote areas, including outback Australia, and are designed to fall out of orbit within a few years once retired.
But more satellites mean more close approaches, and operators must perform large numbers of avoidance manoeuvres.
Astronomers have raised another concern: sunlit satellites leave bright streaks across telescope images and can interfere with radio observations.
Darker coatings and sunshades have been tried, but the growing traffic is changing how scientists plan their observations.
Cleaning up.
International guidelines have long asked operators to remove satellites from busy low orbits within 25 years of the end of a mission.
In 2022 the United States regulator set a stricter five-year rule for satellites it licenses.
Rocket stages are increasingly designed to burn up quickly, and satellites carry fuel to lower themselves at the end of their lives.
Removing existing junk is harder, because every piece is moving fast and tumbling.
Japan's Astroscale has flown missions that approached and inspected a discarded rocket stage, and European projects are developing robotic arms and nets to catch dead satellites.
In Australia, the Australian Space Agency works with industry on space situational awareness, tracking objects to help keep orbits safe.
The key idea: Earth is ringed by dead satellites, rocket stages and fragments travelling so fast that even tiny pieces cause serious damage.
Part three. Telescopes: our eyes on the universe.
In 1610 a hand-made tube of lenses showed Galileo moons circling Jupiter.
Today a mirror a million and a half kilometres away sees galaxies born soon after the Big Bang.
Galileo's first look.
The telescope was invented in the Netherlands around 1608, and within a year the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei had built his own, eventually reaching about 20 times magnification.
Pointing it at the sky, he found mountains and craters on the Moon, countless stars in the Milky Way, and in January 1610 four moons orbiting Jupiter.
He later saw that Venus shows phases like the Moon.
These observations challenged the old belief that everything circled Earth and supported the idea that the planets orbit the Sun.
Light and clear air.
The key feature of a telescope isn't magnification but light-collecting area.
A bigger lens or mirror gathers more light, revealing fainter objects and finer detail.
Large lenses sag and blur colours, so in 1668 Isaac Newton built a reflecting telescope with a curved mirror.
Almost every big research telescope today is a reflector, with mirrors of 8 to 10 metres and 25 to 40 metres under construction.
Earth's atmosphere is a nuisance.
Moving air makes stars twinkle and blurs detail, and water vapour blocks some wavelengths.
So major observatories sit on high, dry sites like Mauna Kea in Hawaii and Chile's Atacama Desert.
Siding Spring Observatory near Coonabarabran, New South Wales, hosts the 3.
9-metre Anglo-Australian Telescope.
Adaptive optics, deformable mirrors that change shape hundreds of times a second, cancel out the blur.
Telescopes in space.
The Hubble Space Telescope launched in April 1990 aboard Space Shuttle Discovery and orbits about 540 kilometres up, above the blurring air.
Its 2.
4-metre mirror was ground slightly the wrong shape, so early images were fuzzy, until astronauts fitted corrective optics in 1993.
Its Deep Field images revealed thousands of galaxies in tiny patches of sky, and its measurements helped pin the universe's age at about 13.
8 billion years and show that its expansion is accelerating.
The James Webb Space Telescope launched on 25 December 2021.
Its 6.
5-metre mirror, made of 18 gold-coated hexagonal segments, unfolded in space.
Webb observes mainly in infrared, which passes through dust and reveals very distant galaxies whose light has been stretched by the universe's expansion.
It orbits about 1.
5 million kilometres from Earth, shaded by a tennis-court-sized sunshield that keeps it extremely cold.
Radio astronomy.
Visible light is only a slice of what the universe sends.
In the 1930s Karl Jansky discovered radio waves coming from the Milky Way, launching radio astronomy.

The CSIRO's 64-metre Parkes dish, opened in 1961 and also known as Murriyang in Wiradjuri, helped pinpoint the first identified quasar, has discovered a large share of known pulsars, and revealed the first fast radio burst, a mysterious millisecond flash.
The Square Kilometre Array will be the world's largest radio telescope, split between two sites with very little radio interference.
SKA-Low is being built in Western Australia's Murchison region, on the traditional lands of the Wajarri Yamaji people, with around 131,000 antennas shaped like small metal Christmas trees.
SKA-Mid, with about 200 dishes, is in South Africa's Karoo.
It aims to study the first stars and galaxies.
Start stargazing.
You don't need expensive gear to follow in Galileo's footsteps.
A decent pair of binoculars shows craters on the Moon, Jupiter's four largest moons as tiny points, and star clusters like the Jewel Box in the Southern Cross.
Get away from city lights and give your eyes 20 minutes to adjust to the dark.
Free apps can identify what you're seeing.
Australia's southern skies are superb, and the Magellanic Clouds, two neighbouring galaxies, are visible to the naked eye.
Many public observatories and astronomy clubs run affordable viewing nights.
The key idea: Galileo's telescope showed Jupiter's moons and the Moon's craters, supporting the idea that planets orbit the Sun.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why does the ISS crew see about 16 sunrises and sunsets a day?
Answer. The station circles Earth about every 90 minutes.
Question two. Why can even a tiny fleck of paint damage a spacecraft in low orbit?
Answer. It moves at about 28,000 km/h.
Question three. What did Galileo's observations of Jupiter's moons and Venus's phases challenge?
Answer. The old belief that everything circled Earth.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
